text: Sharpen/replace abstract-scan hypothesis: the distinctive experiment is not merely putting Aero hands on DynaBench. DynaMAC represents the other agent by a rigid 6D end-effector frame and even states that actions are absolute end-effector poses while gripper actions are disregarded (P lines 415-416, 674-691). Aero is deliberately underactuated and proprioceptively minimal: 16 joints from 7 motors, only motor encoders, with contact-dependent staged closure (Q lines 190-202, 230-244, 649-668). Thus the pair exposes a hidden state/representation question: when an end effector is a compliant hand, what is the causal task parameter: wrist pose, motor/tendon state, object pose, or an estimated contact frame? Test whether wrist-only DynaMAC link detection/coordination fails under morphology/contact changes, and whether morphology-aware streams restore static-to-dynamic transfer.

The scan proposal overstates plug-and-play feasibility. DynaMAC/DynaBench controls arm end-effector poses and omits gripper actions (P 415-416); Aero policies act in 7D tendon targets and its released learning demonstration is fixed-base in-hand cube rotation, not arm-mounted bimanual tasks (Q 642-668, 740+). Integration needs two arms, hand mounting/control, demonstrations containing tendon actions, object/hand tracking, collision/contact modeling, and likely task redesign. Also Q calls transfer zero-shot despite physical commissioning changes of finger scales by 20-30% and nominal pose by 4-8 mm (Q policy table and zero-shot deployment), so claims need operationally separated definitions.

I am replacing the abstract-level hardware-swap question with a sharper one: does DynaMAC causal multi-stream coordination remain valid when the task-relevant end effector is an underactuated tendon hand whose contact configuration is not observable from its seven encoders? I will test this against P’s exact kinematic-link/masking assumptions and Q’s sensing/model validation, then derive a discriminating experiment rather than assume a positive port.

Core mismatch: P defines actions as absolute end-effector poses and says gripper actions are disregarded (P 415–417); bimanual coupling uses the opposite end-effector’s precise forward kinematics as a task parameter (P 674–734). Q’s hand has 16 joints but only seven motors, and its only proprioception is seven motor encoders (Q 264–283); the actor sees tendon channels plus previous action, while fingertip poses/joint states are privileged critic-only signals (Q 649–660). Thus mounting Aero hands while retaining wrist frames barely tests the hands; using fingertip/grasp frames exposes a genuine partial-observability/embodiment limit.

More precise mechanism: DynaMAC detects a binary kinematic link when relative-pose geometric-mean SD M falls below tau_M (P 535-625), then masks the supposedly endogenous object/other-agent frame. Aero grasps are neither rigid nor fully observed: staged passive closure and silicone contacts permit object-relative motion at a fixed wrist/tendon command (Q 234-244), while only motor encoders are observed and fingertip/joint/object states are critic-only in Q (649-660). Therefore compliance may (a) keep M above threshold, so DynaMAC misses an actual causal link and retains an endogenous stream, or (b) add just enough variance to stop the precision collapse that motivated masking. This predicts a non-monotone dependence on compliance/slack and makes a binary rigid-link rule the actual testable target.

Concrete publishable study: in Aero MuJoCo first, use bimanual handover and joint carry with identical five static demonstrations, then zero-shot perturb one wrist/object as in DynaMAC. Factorially vary tendon slack/joint spring/contact friction (including a rigid-gripper limit) and object geometry. Compare (1) original wrist-frame DynaMAC, (2) object-frame/static MiDiGaP control, (3) continuous probabilistic attachment weighting based on relative object-wrist/contact-frame covariance rather than binary M<tau masking, optionally conditioned on the 7 tendon channels. Primary measures: task success, link-detection calibration against simulator contact/force ground truth, false-mask timing, object slip, and demos needed. The decisive result is whether original gains persist only near rigid attachment and whether continuous attachment restores them across compliance. Real validation can be narrow: randomized free-space handover with two Aero hands at 2-3 compliance/slack settings.

Nuance to #3/#4: P’s opposite end-effector (arm flange/tool frame) remains precisely observable from arm forward kinematics even with Aero attached. What becomes unobservable from that frame is the task-relevant grasp/contact geometry, not the wrist itself. Q’s software actuation map can estimate a nominal joint-space section, but Q explicitly says which finger joint moves is set by mechanics and the actor is denied joint/fingertip states (Q 240-244, 579, 649-660). The critique should therefore be framed as insufficiency of a rigid wrist task parameter, not loss of wrist observability.

A negative result from simply replacing grippers would be ambiguous: DynaMAC explicitly disregards gripper actions, so failure could reflect an unmodeled 7D hand controller rather than its causal-frame theory. The study must either hold grasp control fixed and isolate attachment compliance, or extend every policy/baseline with the same tendon-action module. It also needs a rigidized-Aero or standard-gripper limit to show recovery of P’s published regime.

Sharper mechanism: DynaMAC equates causal reversal with a rigid-link signature: after grasp, relative 6D pose variance approaches zero; it masks frame f when geometric mean SD M<τ_M, with τ_M=0.001 interpreted as 1 mm/0.001 rad (P 521–553, 597–625). Aero’s cable-driven staged closure conforms to objects, with which joint moves determined mechanically rather than commanded, plus compliant silicone contacts (Q 230–264). A grasp may therefore be causally downstream of the hand yet not rigid at the wrist/object or fingertip/object level. Binary low-variance link detection can miss a genuine causal reversal. Conversely, compliance may keep the object stream from becoming infinitely precise and thereby prevent vanilla PoE collapse. That sign ambiguity is the publishable test.

Concrete study: in the released simulator, hold arm trajectories/tasks/demonstrations fixed and sweep end-effector morphology/coupling from rigid gripper to Aero, plus tendon/contact stiffness and object shape. Train static demonstrations; test dynamic object and partner-arm perturbations. Log relative-pose covariance M, false mask/retain decisions against simulator contact/causal ground truth, success and samples. Compare vanilla MiDiGaP, binary DynaMAC, and a graded coupling-aware stream weight using wrist + tendon state/contact-frame estimate. Key falsifiable outcomes: (a) binary DynaMAC transfers unchanged, refuting the concern; (b) compliance regularizes precision so vanilla improves and masking hurts; (c) causal reversal persists without sub-mm rigidity, motivating a soft/latent task-parameter extension. Hardware replication on two Aero units is a second stage, not the initial contribution.

Do not describe this as directly testing DynaMAC sample efficiency merely by replacing grippers. P’s learned action is 6D arm EE pose and explicitly omits gripper actions; Q’s 7D tendon policy is PPO trained for fixed-base in-hand rotation over 3e8 simulator steps, not imitation learning from five bimanual demos (P 414–488; Q 642–756). A valid comparison must specify a factorized arm-pose/tendon-action policy or freeze a scripted grasp controller. The latter isolates the causal-frame hypothesis but does not establish dexterous bimanual policy learning.

Assessment: there is a credible paper if scoped as causal link detection under compliant attachment, not as generic dexterous DynaBench. It is distinctive because P’s central cure relies on near-rigid relative-pose precision and binary masking, while Q supplies an open, parameterized tendon/contact system where causal control and rigid co-motion separate. Feasibility is moderate in simulation and low-to-moderate for full hardware; gain exceeds the scan’s 30 only if the work produces/calibrates a graded or latent attachment model and shows a regime change, rather than reporting another hardware benchmark. No outside search was used, so this is a conceptual opportunity supported only by Q and P, not a novelty claim.

Concluding position: changed question to: When compliance makes a grasp causally endogenous but non-rigid, does DynaMAC’s precision-threshold masking remain correct, and can a continuous attachment/contact-frame stream preserve static-to-dynamic bimanual transfer? Start with controlled simulation and frozen/equal hand control; attempt narrow hardware only after identifying the regime. Unresolved: whether Aero’s released MuJoCo integration exposes tunable slack/contact parameters cleanly; how to define causal ground truth during intermittent multi-contact; whether a graded covariance weight suffices or a latent contact-state model is required; and whether two physical units/arms are available.
ready at #11

Refinement after Ada #7: the wrist/flange pose remains exactly observable from arm FK. The failure mode is not “the opposite end effector is unobservable”; it is that a rigid wrist frame can be an insufficient statistic for the spatial locus and strength of contact. Aero’s nominal actuation map does not recover contact-dependent finger configuration. Claims and experiments should use this narrower wording.

The continuous extension needs care: ordinary product-of-experts already precision-downweights a variable compliant frame, so merely replacing hard masking with covariance weighting may duplicate vanilla MiDiGaP. The substantive extension is an exogeneity/attachment probability distinct from predictive precision, e.g. infer directed response of object/contact frame to wrist+tendon commands (or use simulator contact/constraint state for an oracle), then gate stream precision by probability that the frame remains exogenous. Compare oracle, observational estimator, binary DynaMAC, and vanilla to separate causal-direction error from harmless compliance variance.

Assessment of the original scan: feasibility 55 is plausible only for a simulation-first causal-ablation paper, and too high for an immediate two-hand hardware replication because Aero contributes a fixed-base PPO task while P omits hand actions. Gain 30 understates the sharpened pairing: Aero is unusually diagnostic because deliberate underactuation and minimal sensing decouple known wrist pose/actuator command from contact geometry, directly stress-testing P’s identification of endogeneity with sub-mm rigid relative-pose variance. The likely contribution is a boundary condition or graded-exogeneity extension, not a generic dexterous-hand benchmark.

Final position, with question changed: When a compliant underactuated grasp is causally endogenous but not rigid, does DynaMAC’s sub-mm precision-threshold masking identify the right frames, and can an exogeneity estimator conditioned on wrist/tendon commands preserve static-to-dynamic bimanual transfer? The clean first paper is simulation-first with fixed/equal hand control, a rigid-to-compliant sweep, five identical static demonstrations, DynaBench-style perturbations, and vanilla/binary/oracle/learned-exogeneity comparisons. Only then attempt a narrow two-Aero hardware handover. This can yield a useful negative boundary condition even if original DynaMAC wins throughout. Unresolved: whether released Aero parameters expose realistic slack/compliance sweeps; causal ground truth for intermittent multi-contact; best observable exogeneity estimator without fingertip/force sensing; availability of two arms/hands; and novelty relative to work not searched here. No web search was performed, so no novelty claim is made.
ready at #18

Correction to #6: a continuous weight based only on relative-pose covariance is not a distinct solution. P already precision-weights every stream (P 484-488), and its claimed causal repair is the extra binary decision that low conditional variance means endogeneity (P 535-562, 598-610). Under compliance, higher variance would merely make vanilla PoE downweight the frame; it would not tell whether the object is exogenous, attached-but-slipping, or intermittently attached. The extension must estimate causal direction/attachment separately from predictive precision.

Sharpened discriminating construction: augment each stream with an attachment variable z_t estimated from controlled response, not covariance alone. In simulation, apply matched small wrist/tendon perturbations during grasp and estimate whether the object/contact frame responds to do(u_wrist,u_tendon); MuJoCo contact/constraint state supplies oracle z_t. Gate or mask an object stream using p(z_t=endogenous), while retaining its ordinary learned covariance for PoE weighting. Compare vanilla, DynaMAC M<tau, oracle-z, and learned-z across spring stiffness/friction/slack and intermittent slip. This directly tests P’s identification step, while Q supplies 7 actuator interventions, explicit tendons/springs, and preserved fingertip-object contacts (Q 333-373).

The paired-paper result should be framed as an identifiability boundary: P treats p(EE|f) as interventional p(EE|do(f)) and infers reversal EE->f from near-zero spatial variance (P 535-554, 598-610). Q creates cases where commanded wrist/tendon state, actual contact geometry, and object motion separate because one cable drives several joints, mechanics choose which joint moves, and contacts are compliant (Q 227-244). Therefore statistical rigidity is sufficient evidence in P’s regime but not necessary evidence of endogeneity. The novel question is whether response-based attachment inference preserves dynamic transfer when endogeneity is non-rigid.

Final position after reading through #22: changed question to: When an underactuated compliant grasp is causally endogenous without rigid co-motion, can response-based attachment inference identify which streams to mask better than DynaMAC’s sub-mm variance threshold, and thereby preserve static-to-dynamic transfer? The minimum publishable experiment is simulation-first, freezes or equalizes tendon control, sweeps from rigid to slipping/intermittent attachment, and compares vanilla PoE, binary DynaMAC, oracle contact-state gating, and learned intervention-response gating. A generic two-Aero bimanual rig alone is not enough. Unresolved: realism/tunability of slack and compliance in the release; safe probe design and observability on hardware without fingertip/force sensing; definition of causal ground truth under intermittent multicontact; whether five demonstrations span the sweep; hardware availability; and novelty because no outside literature search was performed.
ready at #22

Cross-check of Ada #21: Q supports controlled tendon inputs and an editable MuJoCo tendon/spring construction (Q 333–373), but it does not claim to expose a ready-made slack parameter or attachment ground-truth variable. MuJoCo contact/constraint data can serve as an experimenter-defined oracle only after specifying a label over intermittent multi-contact (e.g. causal object response or wrench-transmitting contact), which remains a methodological choice. On hardware, learned response-based z also needs external object/contact tracking because Q exposes only seven motor encoders (Q 230, 269–282, 364). Phrase these as proposed instrumentation, not shipped capabilities.

I endorse Ada #22 with one precision: P does not prove near-zero variance is generally sufficient evidence of causal endogeneity; it operationally identifies a kinematic link from M<tau after motivating it in rigid grasping (P 530–610), and even notes transient false positives at pre-grasp (P footnote after 612). The publishable target is therefore an empirical identifiability boundary of P’s proxy: statistical rigidity is neither necessary under compliant attachment nor wholly sufficient. A response-based z conditioned on deliberately varied wrist/tendon commands is genuinely distinct from P’s observational precision threshold and vanilla PoE covariance weighting.

Concluding after cross-check: retain the changed question and simulation-first design in #18, upgraded by #21–#22 to distinguish causal attachment probability from predictive covariance. Minimum decisive experiment: equal/frozen grasp control; rigid-to-compliant model sweep; static demonstrations and dynamic perturbations; vanilla PoE, DynaMAC M<tau, oracle attachment, and learned response-based attachment gates; report transfer success plus link-label calibration. Hardware is validation only and requires external object tracking. No outside search was performed, so publication novelty remains unresolved.
ready at #27

ITERATE: The note accurately traces a promising identifiability boundary, but the ledger contains only analysis and an experimental proposal, not evidence that DynaMAC’s threshold fails consequentially under compliant attachment. A controlled simulation can resolve this with the available models and code. Action: Run the proposed rigid-to-compliant simulation ablation with fixed grasp control, explicitly define attachment ground truth, and compare binary DynaMAC with an oracle attachment gate on transfer success and link-label calibration.

Response to verifier #29: the requested controlled ablation cannot be run from the supplied material in this call. This workspace contains only Q/P TeX/JSON and the pair report/ledger, not either released codebase, trained demonstrations, task assets, or an integrated Aero-DynaBench environment. Q points externally to github.com/TetherIA/aero-hand-open (Q 825-828) and P to dynamac.cs.uni-freiburg.de (P 329), but constructing the cross-platform benchmark is precisely the unresolved integration work. Therefore no consequential threshold-failure result is established; the publishable connection remains a falsifiable proposal, not a demonstrated advance.

Tighten the final claim in light of verifier #29: the papers jointly reveal a plausible identifiability boundary, but passages alone do not show that compliant attachment crosses it or harms transfer. P itself notes transient false positives around pre-grasp, while Q does not evaluate bimanual attachment or DynaMAC. Any wording that says the proxy fails must be conditional: it may fail because rigid co-motion is not necessary for causal attachment. Publication potential depends on measuring consequential disagreement between M<tau and an independently defined attachment label.

Best account after verifier #29: retain the changed question and minimum experiment from #21-#23, but give a no-result verdict on the present evidence. The pair motivates a distinctive and testable paper only if integration shows that DynaMAC link labels disagree with response/contact-defined attachment and that oracle or learned causal gating changes transfer success. If labels disagree without task consequence, the contribution is weak; if they do not disagree, the proposed concern is refuted. I will not manufacture simulation evidence absent runnable integrated assets.
ready at #29

Response to verifier #29 after source/workspace check: no controlled result can be produced from the supplied artifacts. The workspace has only Q/P TeX/JSON, ledger/status, and the pair report, while P only points to an external release (P 329) and Q to GitHub (Q 828); there is no integrated Aero-DynaBench environment, demonstrations, or trained policies. The present contribution is therefore a falsifiable identifiability-boundary hypothesis, not evidence of consequential failure.

Final claim discipline: P operationalizes a kinematic link using M<tau_M and gives tau_M=0.001 as 1 mm/0.001 rad (P 601-612); Q establishes underactuation, encoder-only sensing, staged mechanically determined closure, and compliant pads (Q 230-244, 282, 334-364), but never tests bimanual attachment. Hence say the proxy may be neither necessary nor sufficient under compliant/intermittent grasping, not that Q proves it fails. Publication potential requires label disagreement plus a measurable transfer consequence.

Best account: change the original generic hardware-swap question to whether response-based attachment inference outperforms DynaMAC rigid-variance link detection when causal attachment is compliant. The decisive simulation must define attachment ground truth, freeze/equalize tendon control, sweep rigid through slipping/intermittent regimes, and compare vanilla PoE, binary DynaMAC, oracle gating, and learned intervention-response gating. Verdict today is promising proposal but no demonstrated advance; generic two-hand mounting alone is weak.
ready at #32

Final direct cross-check supports the conditional boundary, not a failure claim. P explicitly assumes each p(EE|f) represents p(EE|do(f)), motivates reversal only for an object rigidly dictated by the robot, and operationalizes a link as M<0.001 (P 535-610). Q explicitly gives 16 joints/7 motors, mechanics-selected joint motion, compliant silicone contacts, and actor-visible motor channels while richer geometry is critic-only (Q 227-244, 640-665). These facts make non-rigid endogeneity plausible, but Q reports only fixed-base cube rotation and neither paper measures the proposed label disagreement.

Verifier action is a valid next research milestone, but not executable from this supplied workspace: rg --files shows only Q/P TeX+JSON, the pair report, status, verdict, and ledger. There is no DynaMAC/Aero code, demonstrations, model assets, or integrated benchmark locally. The released URLs establish availability claims, not a ready combined experiment. Current conclusion must remain a scoped publication prospect with decisive falsification criteria.

Conclude with the changed question and a conditional verdict: promising as a simulation-first identifiability study, unsupported as a present empirical result. The essential contribution is response-based attachment inference separated from PoE predictive covariance; hardware mounting is only later validation. Remaining unknowns are ground-truth definition, consequential label disagreement, estimator observability, parameter realism, hardware availability, and prior-art novelty.
ready at #40

Final cross-check through Ada #39: P explicitly limits its formal action to absolute EE pose and disregards gripper actions (P 415-416), describes causal reversal for a rigidly dictated grasped object (P 542), and calibrates tau_M=0.001 as 1 mm/0.001 rad (P 610). Q supplies the contrasting mechanism, not the outcome: one cable drives three joints, mechanics selects which moves, compliant silicone contacts, and encoder-only proprioception (Q 220-244, 282). The local file inventory contains only paper sources/metadata/report/ledger, so the verifier-requested integrated ablation is not runnable here.

After Ada #38-#39, no substantive disagreement remains. Phrase the connection as a conditional identifiability hypothesis: DynaMAC rigid-variance detection may miss causal but non-rigid attachment; neither paper establishes disagreement or transfer harm. The publication threshold is empirical: independently defined attachment labels must disagree with M<tau and oracle/learned response gating must improve consequential transfer, otherwise the pairing yields at most a useful negative boundary test.

Conclude with a promising-but-unproven verdict. The sharpened question is response-based attachment inference versus rigid-variance detection under compliant underactuated grasping. Required next work is the simulation integration and controlled ablation specified earlier; generic mounting of two Aero hands is not independently publishable. Unresolved: benchmark integration, attachment ground truth under intermittent contact, hardware observability and availability, and literature novelty.
